teaser: Taller than a doorway, painted on the floor in 1907: a life at full bloom, with no person in sight.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 315 x 235 cm; tempera on paper mounted on canvas: check.
Ten Largest painted in roughly 40 days in autumn 1907; four working days per painting is the commonly quoted figure: check.
Yellow = masculine, blue = feminine in af Klint's notebooks: standard reading.
'vestalasket' read as vestal + ascetic is an interpretation, hedged in the text.
Guggenheim 2018-19 exhibition: about 600,000 visitors, the museum's most attended show: check.
Museum label says Hilma af Klint Foundation; the works are often shown at Moderna Museet, Stockholm.

lesson.text: A flower opens a little more each hour, and then, for a short while, it is as open as it will ever be. This painting stops the clock at that point. Not the bud, not the wilting: the middle of a life, when everything a person has been growing toward is finally out in the open.

Hilma af Klint called it “Adulthood”. It is the seventh in a set of ten huge pictures that follow a human life from childhood to old age. Not one of them shows a human. She painted the stages of life the way you might chart weather: with shapes, colors and signs.
The two big yellow forms are in contact at exactly one place, and the whole picture balances on it. Tap that place.

spots.title: The meeting point
spots.text: Every curve in the upper form and every black line in the lower one runs into this single point. Above it, something fully opened. Below it, something still closed like a bulb.

lesson.text: An open bloom above, a closed seed below, joined at a pinch like the waist of an hourglass. You can read it as a plant and its root, or as the present resting on what is still to come. Af Klint did not leave a simple key, and that is part of the pleasure.
The painting is about 3.15 m tall and 2.35 m wide (over 10 by 7.5 ft). It is too big for an easel, so she worked with the paper flat on the studio floor, walking around and over it.

The year was 1907 and she was 45, a trained Stockholm painter who earned her living with landscapes and portraits. In private she belonged to a circle of five women who held séances, meetings where they believed they received messages from spirits. One of these voices, she wrote, asked her to paint a great cycle of pictures for a temple.

She began with these ten. She finished all of them in about forty days, which means a wall-sized painting every four days. The medium was tempera, pigment mixed with egg, which dries fast and matte and has to be put down with confidence. There was no room for hesitation.
In 1907, several years before the painters usually credited with inventing abstract art, Hilma af Klint was already making monumental pictures with no recognizable subject.
The big yellow forms carry writing. So does much of the lilac ground around them. She treated a painting as something to be read as well as seen.

lesson.title: Numbers and words
lesson.text: Follow the white inscriptions across the surface.

spots.title: I
spots.text: A Roman numeral one, drawn in white on the left lobe. A white curve sweeps through this side of the form.

spots.title: II
spots.text: Its partner on the right lobe. Between I and II, dashed and solid arcs in white, pink, red and black all cross at the top of the form like the lines of longitude on a globe.

spots.title: III
spots.text: The lower form gets the three. One and two above, three below: two halves producing a third thing.

spots.title: An invented word
spots.text: At the very bottom she writes “vestalasket” in looping script. It is not a Swedish word. It seems to weld together “vestal”, a virgin priestess, and “asket”, an ascetic.

lesson.text: One, two, three. Two principles joining to make a third is the idea that runs through the whole temple cycle. In her notebooks af Klint linked yellow with the masculine and blue with the feminine, and she kept looking for images in which opposites meet and become one.

Around this central drama the lilac field is as busy as pond water under a microscope. That comparison is not far-fetched. She was a keen student of botany, and scientists of her day were filling books with pictures of cells, shells and spores.

spots.title: Red blossoms
spots.text: Heart-shaped red petals grow on thin stems that loop down the left side. They are the most plant-like things here, close to clover or sweet pea.

spots.title: Black rosette
spots.text: A dark flower with a scalloped edge and tiny red loops inside, like a seed head seen from above. It hangs from the same red line as the round red fruit beside it.

spots.title: A spiral
spots.text: In the top left corner a line coils inward like a snail shell. Spirals recur all over her work as a sign of growth and unfolding.

spots.title: Green bodies
spots.text: Along the top edge, dark green masses hold yellow discs, like cells with their nuclei. Two of them pull apart at a narrow neck, as if dividing.

spots.title: The orange egg
spots.text: An orange oval ringed in black, filled with pale yellow curls. It sits just beside the point where bloom and seed touch.

spots.title: Looping script
spots.text: White loops run along like handwriting in an alphabet nobody else knows. Some of her signs are letters she gave private meanings; others stay unexplained.

spots.title: Paired whites
spots.text: Two pale rounded forms stacked like a figure eight, overlaid with thin yellow diagrams. The pairing of two into one repeats here in miniature.

lesson.text: Nothing in this crowd of forms overlaps much or casts a shadow. Everything floats at the same depth on the same flat color, as on a page. That flatness, so natural in a diagram or a child's drawing, was almost unheard of on a canvas this size in 1907.
Af Klint showed these pictures to almost no one. She asked that her abstract work stay unseen until twenty years after her death, believing the public was not ready. She died in 1944.

The wait turned out longer. Her nephew inherited more than a thousand paintings and stacks of notebooks, and for decades they sat in crates. A wide audience first saw her work in 1986, in a Los Angeles exhibition about spirituality in abstract art.
When the Guggenheim Museum in New York gave her a solo exhibition in 2018, about 600,000 people came. It was the most visited show the museum had ever held.

So a picture of ripeness had to wait some eighty years for its own moment. Think of the pinch point again, the open form resting on the closed one. Hilma af Klint spent her life as the lower shape: sealed, patient, full of lines that all lead somewhere.

quiz.question: What stage does this painting represent in the series of ten?
quiz.explanation: The Ten Largest follow life from childhood to old age, and No. 7 is “Adulthood”.

quiz.question: How did af Klint paint a picture this large?
options: With the paper flat on the studio floor
On scaffolding against a church wall
quiz.explanation: It was too big for an easel, so she worked on the floor.

quiz.question: Which Roman numeral marks the lower yellow form?
quiz.explanation: I and II sit on the two lobes above, III on the form below.

quiz.question: In her notebooks, what did af Klint link yellow with?
quiz.explanation: She paired yellow with the masculine and blue with the feminine.

quiz.question: What did she ask regarding her abstract paintings?
options: That they be sold to pay her debts
That they stay unseen until twenty years after her death
quiz.explanation: She believed the public was not ready for them.

quiz.question: What is tempera?
quiz.explanation: It dries fast and matte, which suited her rapid pace.

facts.text: Af Klint finished all ten of the Ten Largest in about forty days.
facts.explanation: That is roughly one wall-sized painting every four days.

facts.text: “Vestalasket”, written at the bottom, is an ordinary Swedish word.
facts.explanation: It is an invented word that seems to combine “vestal” and “ascetic”.

facts.text: The painting shows a man and a woman standing in a garden.
facts.explanation: There are no human figures, only shapes, colors and signs.
